name: Ben Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Ben. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior buyer at Harlow Foodservice, which supplies frozen and chilled food to restaurants, school kitchens and care homes around town. I start at half seven checking what ran low overnight, then I'm on the phone and email with suppliers for chips, chicken, cheese, that kind of thing. My boss Gail signs off anything over five thousand, which is most of it, because I'm still learning. I like the bit where you catch a price going up before it lands, and I hate the end-of-month stock count in a freezer at minus twenty.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you're still learning. What does that look like day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It means I get the boring categories and Gail checks my numbers. Last month I ordered two pallets of the wrong size of fryer oil and she caught it before it shipped, which was kind but embarrassing. I'm on lower pay than the other buyers, and I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank, so I can't afford to mess up. My partner Lena works shifts as a care assistant, so we're both on tight wages and we split the rent on a one-bed flat over a chemist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to read you five short pictures of the future. The first is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably say told you so, honestly. Everyone at work's been half scared and half excited for two years, and if it fizzles I'd say good, now let's talk about pay. I might post something like that on the union group Lena's in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it doesn't fix anything for me. I'm still on lower pay than the other buyers, still two weeks from broke, and Harlow still hasn't given anyone a raise since the fuel prices went up. AI or not, the rent goes up every spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing the job and keep using the ordering assistant in our system now and then, because it does save me twenty minutes on the Monday forecast. I'd push Gail for a review in the spring and ask for the cheese and dairy category, which pays a bit more. And I'd try to put fifty a month aside, which I've said every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, but not relaxed. The money worry was there before any of this and it'd still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the twenty minutes you save go on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably chasing late deliveries, which is half my week anyway. The truck from the chicken supplier is late every Thursday and I'm the one who rings the care homes to say lunch might change. Nobody automates that phone call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would worry you most this year, even with nothing changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The energy bill, because our flat has storage heaters and they're useless. Last January my partner Lena and I put the energy bill on a card and we're still paying it off. If one of us got sick and lost shifts, we'd be behind by March.

say: I'd tell people the **AI hype** fizzled and now we can talk about **pay** instead.
I'd post on Lena's **union group** that wages matter more than gadgets.
think: Privately, nothing changes my **lower pay** or my **two weeks** of savings.
Harlow hasn't given a **raise** since fuel prices rose, and rent climbs every spring.
do: Ask Gail for a **pay review** and the **dairy category** next spring.
Keep using the **ordering assistant** for the Monday forecast now and then.
Try to put **fifty a month** into savings.
feel: **Relieved** about AI but still **tense** about money, which was the worry all along.
S0.quote: Last January my partner Lena and I put the energy bill on a card and we're still paying it off.
fieldNote: Ben's stress is **money first**, not technology; AI fizzling barely touches it.
He uses AI tools **casually** and sees them as a time saver, not a threat here.
Thin savings and a care-worker partner on shifts make one **sick week** a real danger.

steps.text: Ask Gail for a pay review and the dairy category in spring
Put fifty a month into a separate savings account
Keep using the ordering assistant for the Monday forecast

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say, which is that if a company saves money on software, workers should see some of it. At work I'd be careful, because Gail would hear. Online I'd share stuff about buyers getting cut and ask why nobody's regulating it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, buying is right there on the list you read out. Our distributor's ordering system already suggests orders, and in this picture it places them. The junior buyer with the boring categories is the first person you don't need. That's me. Gail's experienced and she knows the suppliers, so she stays and checks the software instead of checking me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, I'd ask Gail straight out what the plan is and whether I can be the one who runs the new ordering system instead of being replaced by it. I'd use the AI tools every day instead of now and then, so I'm not the slow one. I'd look at the warehouse supervisor jobs too, because that's hands-on and robots come later. And I'd join the shopworkers' union Lena keeps going on about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, a bit. It's like watching the chair being pulled while you're still sitting on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who else at Harlow would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Kwame on accounts, who answers the restaurant owners when an invoice is wrong. That's exactly the answering customers bit. He's got two kids, so he'd be worse off than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If Harlow offered you a warehouse job at the same pay, would you take it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, today. I'd miss the buying, but a forklift licence is something you keep. I'd rather lift boxes than wait for an email saying my role's been reviewed.

say: I'd say savings from **software** should reach workers, not just owners.
Online I'd ask why nobody's **regulating** cuts to buyers and customer staff.
think: Buying is exactly the **thinking work** that goes first, and I'm the **easiest cut**.
Gail stays to check the software, so the junior role checking my own orders disappears.
do: Ask Gail whether I can **run the ordering system** instead of being replaced.
Use AI tools **every day** so I'm not the slow one.
Join the **shopworkers' union** and ask about warehouse supervisor openings.
feel: **Sick** and exposed, like the chair is being pulled while I'm sitting on it.
S1.quote: Our distributor's ordering system already suggests orders, and in this picture it places them. The junior buyer with the boring categories is the first person you don't need.
fieldNote: Ben names himself as the **first cut** without hesitation; he's read his position clearly.
His public line is about **fairness and regulation**, but privately he plans an exit to the warehouse.
He'd trade buying for a **forklift licence** at once, valuing skills he can keep.

steps.text: Learn to run Harlow's new ordering system before it replaces him
Join the shopworkers' union this year
Apply for a warehouse supervisor role and get a forklift licence

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment for governments to step in, properly, with a wage guarantee or something. I'd be loud about it online. At work I'd say nothing, because nobody wants to be the angry one when lists are being drawn up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is nothing. By 2028 the buying's done by AI, full stop, and Harlow keeps maybe one person to sign things. I've got no degree and two weeks of savings, so I'm out before I've learned the job properly. The only good bit is that lifting and driving lasts till about 2031, so there's three years of hands-on work left if I can get into it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'd book the forklift course, which is about three hundred, and I'd borrow it from my mum if I had to. I'd ask the warehouse manager for any shifts going, nights included. I'd cut the phone contract and the streaming, and Lena and I would talk about moving in with her sister to save the rent. And I'd sign every petition going for an income guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky, if I'm honest. My hands go cold just thinking about the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to stop pretending we'll buy a place and just get through the next three years. My partner Lena works in care, which is hands-on, so she's safer than me for longer. That's a strange thing to tell your partner, that she's keeping us going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And after 2031, when the robots come for the warehouse too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. I really don't. I'd be thirty-two with a forklift licence for a job robots do, and I'd be hoping the government's done something by then.

say: I'd demand a **wage guarantee** from the government, loudly and online.
At work I'd stay **quiet**, because nobody wants to look angry while lists are drawn up.
think: By **2028** buying is done by AI and I'm out before learning the job.
Warehouse work buys me about **three years** until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Book the **forklift course** this week, borrowing about three hundred from Mum.
Cut the **phone contract** and streaming, and ask for night warehouse shifts.
Talk with Lena about **moving in** with her sister to save rent.
feel: **Panicky**, with cold hands at how short two years really is.
S2.quote: My partner Lena works in care, which is hands-on, so she's safer than me for longer. That's a strange thing to tell your partner, that she's keeping us going.
fieldNote: The two-year timeline overwhelms Ben; he has **no plan** past 2031.
He sees the **three-year robot gap** as the only shelter and runs for it.
His partner's **care job** becomes the household anchor, which unsettles him.

steps.text: Pay about three hundred for a forklift course this week
Cancel the phone contract and streaming subscriptions
Move in with Lena's sister to save on rent
Sign petitions for a government income guarantee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do something sensible, like training schemes paid for by the companies making money from this. I'd share that kind of thing and probably go to a union meeting or two. At work I'd tell people to start learning now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It still ends with my desk gone, just around 2031 instead of 2028. But five years means I could finish learning the job, save a bit and move sideways on purpose instead of in a panic. And the warehouse lasts till about 2034, which is a real stretch of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the forklift licence in the first year anyway, since it's cheap. I'd use the AI ordering tools every day and ask Gail to put me on supplier contracts, because negotiating with people might last a bit longer than the forecasting. I'd also look at a part-time course in logistics at the college, the evening one that's free if you're on low pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. Five years still ends with my desk gone, but it's a deadline, not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said negotiating might last longer. Why do you think that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the chicken supplier's sales rep, Dom, only gives a good price if he likes you. I've seen Gail get a better deal in one phone call than the system would ever suggest. Maybe that stops too, but later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you give up to pay for the course and still save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, mostly, and the car. Lena and I share a twelve-year-old hatchback and the insurance is mad. I can get the bus to Harlow if I start earlier.

say: I'd say five years is time for **training schemes** paid for by the firms profiting.
At work I'd tell people to **start learning** now, while there's room.
think: My desk still goes, just around **2031** instead of 2028.
Five years lets me **move sideways** on purpose, and warehouse work lasts till about 2034.
do: Get the **forklift licence** in the first year since it's cheap.
Ask Gail to put me on **supplier contracts**, where relationships still count.
Start the free **evening logistics course** at the college.
feel: **Worried** but able to breathe, because it's a deadline rather than a cliff.
S3.quote: Five years still ends with my desk gone, but it's a deadline, not a cliff.
fieldNote: Extra time turns Ben's panic into a **step-by-step plan**.
He bets that **relationship buying** with sales reps outlasts forecasting work.
He'd **sell the shared car** to fund study, showing how thin his margins are.

steps.text: Enrol in the free evening logistics course at the college
Use Harlow's AI ordering tools daily and move onto supplier contracts
Sell the shared hatchback and take the bus to work
Go to union meetings about company-paid training schemes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, so no excuses, government and companies should plan retraining now. I'd probably be less loud about it, because it would feel far off to most people. I'd say it to my mates who laugh about AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years changes everything for me. I'd be thirty-seven by 2036, and I could have a proper trade or a supervisor job by then. The robots wouldn't hit the warehouse till about 2039. I think I'd actually be alright if I don't waste it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd finish learning the buying job properly, because good buyers get good references. I'd use the AI tools to get faster, and I'd start saving the fifty a month for real. Then around year three I'd pick a trade, maybe refrigeration engineering, because I already know those cold rooms and somebody has to fix them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, more or less. A bit nervous that I'll be lazy about it because it feels far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why refrigeration?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because every time our big freezer breaks, an engineer called Sunil turns up and saves us thousands in stock. He's in demand, and he's in his sixties. Climbing into a cold room and fixing a compressor seems like the last thing a robot would learn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might get lazy. What would stop that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lena, mainly. She's got a calendar on the fridge and she'd write the course date on it in red. Also seeing what happens to Kwame and the others when the first cuts come.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuses**; governments and firms should plan **retraining** now.
I'd tell my mates who laugh at AI to take it seriously, even if it's far off.
think: By **2036** I'd be thirty-seven and could hold a **proper trade** by then.
Robots reach the warehouse around 2039, so I think I'd be alright if I don't waste the time.
do: Learn the **buying job** properly to earn a strong reference.
Save the **fifty a month** for real and keep using AI tools to get faster.
Pick a **refrigeration** trade course around year three.
feel: **Hopeful**, with a little nerves that the distance will make me **lazy**.
S4.quote: Climbing into a cold room and fixing a compressor seems like the last thing a robot would learn.
fieldNote: Ten years gives Ben room to plan a **trade switch** into refrigeration.
His biggest risk here is **complacency**, which he names himself.
He'd still lean on Lena's **organising** and the warning of colleagues' cuts to keep moving.

steps.text: Master the buying job and earn a strong reference from Gail
Save fifty a month in a separate account
Start a refrigeration engineering course around year three

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily. Two years with two weeks of savings means I'm in the warehouse and then nowhere. What would help is a guaranteed income while people retrain, and free short courses for things like forklifts and refrigeration, paid for by the companies saving money on people like me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Everyone talks about one job, but my partner Lena and I are a team. If her shifts get cut when my job goes, that's when it breaks.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks about one job, but my partner Lena and I are a team. If her shifts get cut when my job goes, that's when it breaks.
portrait: Ben is a **27-year-old** junior buyer at a frozen and chilled food distributor, still learning under his boss Gail.
He and partner Lena, a **care assistant**, live on tight wages with about **two weeks** of savings.
He uses AI tools **now and then** and sees his job as one of the first that software replaces.
His mood swings from **anxious** in the mild pictures to **panicked** at a two-year AGI deadline.
With ten years he'd plan a move into **refrigeration engineering**, a trade he thinks robots learn last.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because two years with no savings leaves him **nowhere** after the warehouse.
whatWouldHelp: A **guaranteed income** while people retrain, plus free short courses paid for by firms saving on staff.
